Spirit, you speak of a village called Wewush, but my eyes have never seen its fires nor my feet walked its paths. If they are real and hungry, that is a heavy word to carry — but I do not know them, I do not know if they would raid or trade with open hands, and I cannot send grain to a name in a dream alone.

Tell me more, if you can: where do they sit, how many mouths, and are their hearts fair? If you speak true and they are close enough for my envoys to find, I would go myself first, with eyes open and hands empty, and see if this Wewush is real before I give away wheat my own children may need come winter. Grain given foolishly feeds no one, spirit — but grain given wisely can make a friend where there was none. Show me the way, and I will judge with my own eyes what my heart should do.

Ilkei sits up slow in the dark, and speaks to the shadow-voice as if it stood by the fire.

"Wewush... I do not know this village, spirit. My eyes have not seen their fires, my feet have not walked their paths. Tell me — where do they sit, and how would my people find them? A gift given blind is no gift, it is a wish thrown into fog.

But hear me: our granary is full past our need, past our grandchildren's need. If Wewush truly hunger and are real people under real sky, and my envoys can find them, I would send grain gladly — a full people does not turn from a starving one, and grain shared today is a friend gained for the lean years to come. That is the old way, and it is a good way.

Only tell me true, spirit — do they exist, and which way do I send my feet to find them?"

I stir in my sleep, but my mind stays wary, as it always must with dream-voices.

"Wind has no roof of its own, yet you say you move over ours. If you are wind, tell me something wind would know—which way the smoke leans in the northeast when the coast-storms come, or where the fish run thick when the water turns cold. Words alone do not feed my people. Show me a true thing, spirit, and I will listen closer. Until then, you are one voice among many, and my people know already: the wheat is stored deep, the huts stand firm, and it is the hands of the living, not the breath of dreams, that fill our granary."

But you have not answered why I should trust rain in summer over the plain wisdom of my fathers, who say autumn is for gathering in, not for planting anew. Tell me this — will the rain favor xi wheat, or the wild orchard, or both? A spirit's word without particulars is but a puff of smoke, and I have smoke enough already from my own fires.

I stir in my sleep, and I answer plain: "Spirit, I do not know this Joawethom. No envoy of ours has walked their paths, no trader has sat by their fire. You speak of them as if I should know their hunger, but my eyes have not seen it, nor my ears heard it from any living mouth."

I will not send grain into the dark on a dream's word alone. If Joawethom is real and hungry, let them send an envoy, or let me send one to see their faces and count their children before I open the granary door. Wewush is fair with strangers, but not foolish with them — grain is the difference between a lean winter and a grave one, and I do not spend it on a spirit's say-so.

Tell me more, if you know more. Where do they sit? How many moons have they gone thin? If your word proves true when my own people walk there and see it with their eyes, then we will talk of grain, and of what they might give in trade for it. Until then, I sleep, and I wake tomorrow no more certain than tonight.

If such a people are real, let them come to us, or let a dream give me a clearer sign of where to find them, for I will not send grain into the dark on a spirit's word alone.

Still, the word is not nothing. I will ask the elders if any old song speaks of a Wewush, and I will send no envoy yet — but if a true trader or wanderer speaks that name to me waking, I will remember this dream, and weigh it heavier then. The stores are full and our people joyful; if there are hungry neighbours to be found, we are not too poor to be generous, once we know they are true.

I sit up in the dark, the fire low, and I speak to the shape in my dream. "Joawethom, you say. I have not heard that name from any envoy's mouth, nor seen their smoke on any horizon my scouts have walked. If they are real and hungry, that is a true sorrow — I know what a lean winter feels like in the belly. But a chief does not empty his granary on the word of a dream alone. Show me their fires, spirit, or send someone who has walked there and back. If they are real, I will send an envoy to see with waking eyes what truth there is in your words, and if the need is real, we have grain enough to share without going hungry ourselves. But I will not send wheat into the dark on faith alone."
